extracted.intended_audience: educated British political public, members of Parliament, and readers interested in the French Revolution (late 18th-century pamphlet audience)
extracted.subtask_description: A political pamphlet-style reflection evaluating the French Revolution and the conduct of London societies, offering normative standards for judging revolutions, public speech, and civic organizations. It argues for prudence, constitutional preservation, institutional safeguards, and transparency in public political acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve constitution; prefer reparation to ruin
rubrics_metrics.description: A legitimate political response is to correct and legalize defects in government rather than to change the fundamental order of the state. In England the Revolution was 'in truth and substance, and in a constitutional light, a revolution, not made, but prevented.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not impair monarchy or foundational institutions; remove anomalies and settle doubtful questions while keeping the constituent parts of the state (lords, commons, corporations, electors, law, revenue, magistracy) intact. Act with reparation, not with a mind to 'ruin.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain military unity and discipline under single authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Armies should be put under a single authority with a common oath of fidelity and kept under regular inspection so they are instruments of the state and not of faction or mutiny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid dividing the army with competing principles of obedience; centralize command and ensure annual oversight. This prevents armies becoming instruments of treason or arbitrary violence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish revolutions by circumstances; avoid abstract comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: One must not conflate different revolutions (e.g., England's and France's) because the circumstances shape whether resistance or management is appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate political change contextually — what was arbitrary power here may differ from there; the same label ('revolution') can cover opposite actions. Circumstances give political principles their 'distinguishing color and discriminating effect.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not congratulate new liberty until institutions are secure
rubrics_metrics.description: Suspend public congratulations on a newly proclaimed liberty until it is shown how liberty is combined with stable government and social institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check that liberty is accompanied by: a permanent body for its residence, effective public force, discipline and obedience of armies, a well-distributed and effective revenue, morality and religion, solidity and security of property, peace and order, and suitable civil and social manners. Without these, liberty may be fleeting or harmful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power in inexperienced hands must be observed before endorsement
rubrics_metrics.description: Newly acquired power in inexperienced persons is dangerous; prudent observers should examine how such power is used before declaring support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch the actions of the new rulers and those who appear most active—they may not be the real movers. Better to be cautious and 'despised for too anxious apprehensions than ruined by too confident a security.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Pulpit and church should avoid partisan politics
rubrics_metrics.description: Sermons and religious pulpits ought not to be vehicles for political partisanship; the Church's role is the 'healing voice of Christian charity.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political harangues from the pulpit are dangerous and novel; mixing religion with party politics corrupts both. Clergy should be moderate and avoid using religious authority to propagate political doctrines or to set up partisan ecclesiastical ventures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public declarations must show authorship and accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: Resolutions or votes that stand solely on unnamed authority are suspect; political statements issued by societies should disclose who speaks and with what legitimacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Signatures should be annexed to public instruments so the world may judge how many endorse them and the value of those opinions from the signatories' knowledge, experience, or authority. Anonymous or ambiguous corporate-sounding addresses invite deceit and political stratagem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arguments should be evidence-based, not mere appeals to authority
rubrics_metrics.description: A piece of argument is judged by its reasoning and evidence; a resolution founded only on authority (a vote or declaratory resolution) is weak and may mislead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If what is sent forth were an argument it would matter less whose it is; but when it is a mere vote or resolution, its force is only the authority of the few who signed it—this can be a political stratagem and even a kind of fraud.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid abstract political theorizing detached from concrete circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: Political maxims taken in the abstract may be harmless or noble, but their practical effect depends on the circumstances in which they are applied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not apply universal doctrines (e.g., 'liberty is good') without examining local, historical, social, and institutional conditions; abstractions can produce perverse outcomes when mixed with the passions and situations of real peoples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine equivocations and slippery constructions in political language
rubrics_metrics.description: Political writers often use ambiguous phrasing or equivocation to make dangerous doctrines appear harmless; such constructions must be exposed and criticized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Probe the plain meaning and direct tendency of doctrines (for example, the claim that the king 'owes his crown to the choice of his people') and beware of interpretations offered as evasions or subterfuges that render propositions nugatory or secretly radical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Declare fundamental political rights with caution
rubrics_metrics.description: Bold claims about new 'rights' (e.g., to choose governors, cashier them, frame government) asserted in the name of the people may belong only to a faction and can threaten existing constitutional order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether proclaimed rights truly represent the body of the people or only a particular faction; resist practical assertions of such claims when they conflict with established law and public will, as they may provoke resistance and civil danger.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve established religious institutions while removing intolerance
rubrics_metrics.description: The Church and its orders, estates, and functions should be preserved and secured, but cleared of intolerant practices that are disgraceful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reform should aim to secure the Church's efficiency and remove its weakness (intolerance), not to impair its majesty, splendor, or social role. Religious stability contributes to public order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public political societies must avoid usurping diplomatic or governmental roles
rubrics_metrics.description: Clubs and societies should not act as if they are corporate, authorized bodies of the nation or as committees for foreign governments, thereby giving themselves undue diplomatic weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Societies should avoid addressing foreign assemblies in ambiguous terms that suggest they speak for parts of the nation; such behavior misleads foreign bodies and is improper without explicit legal authority from one's government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Praise and adulation can corrupt public judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Excessive public praise and adulation—particularly premature congratulations for political change—can corrupt both the giver and receiver and blind people to dangers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hold back fulsome public applause until the real effects of political change are visible; avoid turning early enthusiasm into incentives for reckless or violent conduct.
